key_insight: Accurate medical information in peer-to-peer health narratives is not automatically safe, because factual alignment and health risk can be largely independent.
clinical_relevance: For online health content moderation, fact-checking alone can miss risky advice and overblock harmless but divergent narratives, so risk-aware review is needed.
method: Computed Narrative Truth Distance for epistemic divergence and Narrative Risk Score for health-risk potential using non-overlapping feature sets.
Mapped content into a 4-quadrant classification to separate aligned/risky and divergent/safe narratives.
evidence_signal: The two scores shared only 4.9% of variance (r = 0.222, p < 0.001), and 39.6% of narratives fell into off-diagonal quadrants that single-axis systems misclassify.
watch_item: The framework depends on the quality of risk and truth feature engineering, so real-world deployment would need careful validation across topics, platforms, and populations.
paper_title: The Online Health Safety Gap: Consensus Alignment Does Not Imply Safety in Peer-to-Peer Health Narratives.
